Pathology of the Heart IPTH LEC · LE 2 · Trans 5A · Dr. Socorro Yanez

Lesson at a Glance

This lecture reviews the normal heart (size, layers, conduction system, blood supply, valves), the cardiovascular pathology of aging, the six pathophysiologic mechanisms of cardiac dysfunction, and then focuses on Congestive Heart Failure (CHF): its definition, compensatory mechanisms, pathophysiology, etiology, and types.

Must Know= red-exclamation (❗) or lecturer-emphasized (📣) content
Study note= short aid added for recall, not a lecture statement

I. Normal vs. Abnormal Heart p. 1

A. Normal Heart

  • Conical shaped organ with tapered end towards the apex
  • Weight varies with body habitus and is approximately the size of your fist
ParameterNormal value
Average weight of adult heartFemale: 250-300 gm
Male: 300-350 gm
Thickness of the ventricular wallRight ventricle (RV): 0.3-0.5 cm
Left ventricle (LV): 1.3-1.5 cm
  • Normal dimensions are important in order to assess problems of: cardiomegaly, cardiac dilatation, hypertrophy, atrophy

B. Abnormal Heart

TermDefinition
HypertrophyIncrease in heart weight or ventricular thickness
DilationEnlarged chamber size
CardiomegalyIncrease in cardiac weight or size due to hypertrophy and/or dilation
AtrophyDecrease in cardiac size causing a decrease in function
Common in aging and long-standing effects of ischemic heart disease (IHD)
Key pointHypertrophy and dilation reflect compensatory changes in response to volume and/or pressure overloads.

II. Anatomy of the Heart p. 1-2

  • Highly specialized muscular organ located at the left side of the thoracic cavity
  • 4 chambers
    • Right atrium: receives deoxygenated blood from systemic veins
    • Left atrium: receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins
    • Right ventricle and left ventricle
  • Divisions of the chambers
    • IVS and interatrial septum: divide the heart into left and right sides
    • Mitral and tricuspid valves (atrioventricular valves): divide the heart into atrial and ventricular chambers
  • Differences in wall thickness are due to variations in the amount of myocardium
    • Reflects the amount of work and mechanical force required to pump blood
    • Atria: thin-walled chambers that receive blood from the veins
    • Ventricles: thick-walled muscular chambers that forcefully pump blood out of the heart

A. Layers of the Heart

The wall of the heart is composed of 3 layers: Epicardium · Myocardium · Endocardium

Pericardium ("pericardial sac")

  • Membrane that directly surrounds the heart and defines the pericardial cavity
  • Outer fibrous pericardium: tough, dense connective tissue that protects the heart and maintains its position in the thorax
  • Inner serous pericardium (more delicate)
    • Parietal pericardium: fused to the fibrous pericardium
    • Epicardium (inner visceral pericardium): fused to the heart and is part of the heart wall
  • Pericardial cavity: between the epicardium and the pericardium, contains approximately 20-40 mL lubricating serous fluid

Myocardium

  • Makes up bulk of the heart: specialized striated muscle cells called cardiac myocytes
    • Pumping function through coordinated contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole)
  • Sarcomere: functional intracellular contractile unit of cardiac muscle
    • Important proteins: Actin and Myosin
    • Regulatory proteins: Troponin and Tropomyosin → sensitive and specific diagnostic markers for cardiac injury (e.g., diagnosis of AMI)
  • LV myocytes produce more robust contractile forces compared to RV myocytes
  • Endocrine functions
    • Atrial cardiomyocytes → atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) in cytoplasmic storage granules
    • Ventricular myocytes → B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP)
    • Both released in response to stretch → arterial vasodilation, natriuresis and diuresis

Endocardium

  • Similar to the endocardium of blood vessels. Subendocardial layer is made up of loose connective tissue

B. Specialized Myocytes: Conduction System

  • Specialized excitatory and conducting myocytes that regulate heart rate and rhythm
  • Electrical impulses are sensitive to: neural inputs (vagal stimulation), adrenergic agents, hypoxia, potassium concentration
SA node
junction of right atrial appendage and SVC
Cardiac pacemaker
→
AV node
right atrium along interatrial septum
Gatekeeper: slows signal so atria contract before ventricles
→
Bundle of His
connects right atrium to ventricular septum
→
Right and left bundle branches + Purkinje
ventricles contract synchronously

C. Blood Supply

The heart has high metabolic function and is highly sensitive to low levels of oxygen and hypoxia.

Epicardial coronary arterySupplies
Left anterior descending (LAD)Anterior ⅔ of the IVS
Anterior portion of the LV
Entire apex of the heart, circumferentially
Left circumflex (LCX)
arises from the left (main) coronary artery		Posterior, lateral and left aspect of the LV
Right coronary arteryPosterior ⅓ of septum
Inferior and posterior wall of right ventricle
❗ Must Know: Ischemic Heart Disease1 of the most important disease in modern urban population.
There is a significant underlying disorder of the coronary artery vessels due to obstruction of the blood flow either by:
  • Occluding thrombus
  • Significant luminal deposition by an atheroma

D. Heart Valves

  • 4 cardiac valves: Tricuspid · Pulmonary · Mitral · Aortic
  • Important in maintaining unidirectional blood flow
  • Valve function and competence depends on:
    • Mobility, pliability, and structural integrity of leaflets (AV valves) and cusps (semilunar valves)
    • Integrity of cuspal attachments: AV valves attach via chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, anchored by an annular fibrous ring
Diseases of the valves produceRegurgitant functional change: blood returns or flows backward.
Obstructive functional change: limit of blood forward flow.

Normal aortic valve

GrossMicroscopic: 3 layers of the normal valve
  • Poorly vascular dense and loose CT
  • 3 thin, transparent, smooth delicate cusps, devoid of nodules and vegetations
  • Cusps separated by commissures
  • Coronary artery orifices just above
  • Fibrosa: dense collagenous core at outflow surface, provides mechanical force and integrity
  • Spongiosa: core of loose connective tissue
  • Ventricularis or Atrialis: rich in elastin, name depends on which chamber it faces, provides leaflet recoil
  • Innermost lining: single layer of endothelial cells
  • Normal leaflets have only scant blood vessels limited to the proximal portion
  • Valve endothelium does not express ABO or histocompatibility antigens → can easily be transplanted

III. Cardiovascular Pathology of Aging p. 4-5

  • Aging: gradual decline of all physiological functions due to a decrease in repair mechanisms, senescence, progressing to death
  • Most forms of heart disease become more prevalent with each advancing decade

Table 1. Changes in the Aging Heart Must Know

LocationChanges
ChambersIncreased left atrial cavity size
Decreased left ventricular cavity size
Sigmoid-shaped ventricular system
ValvesAortic valve calcific deposits
Mitral valve annular calcific deposits
Fibrous thickening of leaflets
Buckling of mitral leaflets towards left atrium
Lambl's excrescences
Epicardial coronary arteriesTortuosity
Diminished compliance
Calcific deposits
Atherosclerotic plaque
MyocardiumDecreased mass
Increased subepicardial fat
Brown atrophy
Lipofuscin deposition
Basophilic degeneration
Amyloid deposits
AortaDilated ascending aorta with rightward shift
Elongated (tortuous) thoracic aorta
Sinotubular junction calcific deposits
Elastic fragmentation and collagen accumulation
Atherosclerotic plaque

Mitochondrial changes
Pigment depositions: lipofuscin
Exam trapFatty streak in the coronary aorta is NOT an expected aging finding.
It is seen in infants and as a precursor lesion. Formative quiz key

Progressive Degeneration with Aging

  • Structural changes can involve: myocardium, cardiac conduction system, valves, endocardium
  • Degeneration includes: loss of elasticity, fibrotic changes in the valves, infiltration with amyloid, deposits of wear-and-tear pigment (morphologic expression of oxidative stress)
Greatest impactThe age-associated change with greatest impact: contractility of the heart's left ventricular wall.
  • Structural and functional changes are characterized by: vascular stiffening, increased LV wall thickness, hypertrophy, fibrosis, alterations in cardiac diastolic function
  • Pumping capacity is reduced with age
    • Rather than atrophy, an age-related increase of LV posterior wall thickness of approximately 25% has been found in the 7th decade
  • ↑ heart mass is mostly due to an increase in average myocyte size, whereas the total number of myocardial cells decline
  • The heart tends to enlarge slightly, with thicker walls and slightly larger chambers
  • Age-related stiffening → LV with reduced compliance → can lead to diastolic heart failure
    • Accelerated in the presence of HPN, DM, and obesity

Valvular and Vascular Changes

  • Valvular changes reported in all valves, with the greatest change in the aortic valve
  • Age-related increase in valvular circumference: greatest in the aortic and mitral valves
    • Aortic valve stenotic lesions are common in elderly due to deposition of calcium nodules
    • Lambl's excrescences are common
  • Clinical heart murmurs are detected
  • Arteries lose elastic tissue → stiffer and less resilient aorta → increased tortuosity
  • Complicated atherosclerosis in coronary arteries → vascular occlusion → hypertension and ischemia
  • Varicosities are common in the elderly
❗ Must Know: Lambl's excrescencesThin filiform outgrowths on the aortic valve and at the root of the aorta.
Usually located in the cooptation of commissure sites on the valve surface.
Microscopic: acellular and poorly vascular fibroelastic tissue, may be densely hyalinized, covered by endothelium.
Hallmark feature: poorly vascularized, dense, fibrous CT.

Myocardial Subcellular Changes

  • Nuclear enlargement with nuclear membrane invaginations
  • Mitochondrial changes: size, shape, crystal patterns, matrix density
  • Fatty infiltration or degeneration
  • Vacuole formation with progressive accumulation of lipofuscin pigments
Subcellular changes
→
Decrease in cellular activity
altered homeostasis, protein synthesis, degradation rates

Figure 9. Morphological Effects of Aging

PanelWhat to notice
Left topLambl's excrescences: thin filiform outgrowths on aortic valve / aortic root

IV. Cardiac Pathology p. 5-6

A. Epidemiology

  • CVD is the #1 cause of death globally (WHO / AHA 2018), estimated 17.9 million deaths each year
  • 4 out of 5 CVD deaths are due to heart attacks and strokes
  • 75% of CVD occur in low- and middle-income countries
  • 85% of CVD deaths are due to preventable AMI and cerebrovascular accidents

B. Six Pathophysiologic Mechanisms of Cardiac Dysfunction Must Know

MechanismDescriptionExamples from lecture
1. Pump failureInability to contract adequately → low CO during systole
Failure of relaxation → inadequate filling during diastole		Massive MI → pump failure and cardiogenic shock
2. Obstruction to blood flowCoronary artery obstruction (atherosclerotic plaque or thrombosis) or obstruction within the heart chambers when a valve becomes stenotic
Secondary changes: chamber dilation or hypertrophy		Congenital pulmonary stenosis
Acquired aortic calcific stenosis
3. Regurgitation flowOrganic abnormalities in an incompetent valve
Portion of CO flows backwards → increased volume and work overload to affected atria or ventricle		Mitral valve prolapse: floppy incompetent valve → blood returns to atrium → atrial dilatation
4. Shunted flowBlood diverted from one part of the heart to another through an opening or defect
Congenital or acquired
Causes volume and pressure overload on the chamber where blood is shunted		VSD: blood shunted left → right due to pressure gradient differences
5. Cardiac conduction disordersUncoordinated generation or transmission of impulse → non-uniform and inefficient contraction, can be lethalAtrial or ventricular fibrillation
6. Rupture of heart or major vesselFatal hemorrhage within the pericardium (cardiac tamponade) or adjoining body cavitiesGunshot wound of LV
Aortic dissection
Rupture of myocardium due to transmural MI
Study note"Pump · Obstruct · Regurgitate · Shunt · Conduct · Rupture" = the 6 mechanisms in lecture order.

V. Congestive Heart Failure p. 6-7

A. Definition Must Know

AHA / American Cardiology GuidelineHeart failure is a complex clinical syndrome that can result from any structural or functional cardiac disorder that impairs the ability of the ventricle to refill or eject blood.
It is largely a clinical diagnosis based on careful history and physical examination.
  • Heart failure is a syndrome, and not a disease
    • Diagnosis relies on a compendium of clinical signs and symptoms, laboratory information, and the pathophysiologic mechanism
  • Final common pathway of many heart diseases, the common end stage of many cardiovascular diseases
  • Pathophysiologic state where the heart is unable to maintain an output sufficient for the metabolic requirements of tissues and organs
  • Commonly called Congestive Heart Failure: a fully progressive condition with poor prognosis
  • Often emerges insidiously from the cumulative effects of chronic work overload
Simple definitionA state that develops when the heart fails to maintain an adequate cardiac output to meet the demands of the body.

Case Scenario: Clinical Prototype of CHF

35/F, RHD with MV and AV stenosis since age 15, admitted for difficulty of breathing.

FindingMeaning
History of RHD with multi-valvular stenosisUnderlying cardiac condition that predisposes to present problems
Difficulty of breathing / shortness of breathDyspnea
Sleeps sitting up on two pillowsOrthopnea: inability to sleep without sitting on two pillows
Worsening over 6 months = disease progression
Easy fatigability, SOB upon climbing stairsExertional dyspnea
PE: ↑ HR, ↑ RR, bi-basal rales, bilateral leg edemaTachycardia, tachypnea
X-ray: cardiomegaly, bilateral pulmonary edemaGeneralized edema involving the lungs and lower extremities
❗ Must KnowThe absence of fever is important information to rule out an infectious/inflammatory cause.

B. Epidemiology

  • Prevalence: 5.8 million in the USA, 64.3 million worldwide, IR 8.52/1000 (Global Health Data Exchange, 2018)
  • Heart failure poses the largest burden after 60 years of age, increasing due to the growing population aged 70 and older

C. Normal Cardiac Output

CO = Stroke Volume x Heart Rate
= 70 mL x 70 beats/min = 4,900 mL/min or 4.9 L/min
Range: 4-6 L/min (normal individual at rest)
  • Stroke volume: volume of blood ejected during ventricular contraction, approximately 70 mL/beat
  • Healthy adult CO at rest averages about 5 L/min
  • CO is an important parameter of the efficiency of blood delivery and an indirect component of how efficiently the heart meets the body's demands
  • In CHF, CO may be insufficient to support simple activities of daily living, nor increase to meet demands of moderate exercise
Heart failure involves an interplay of 2 factors1. Inability of the failing heart to maintain sufficient cardiac output.
2. Recruitment of compensatory mechanisms to maintain cardiac reserve and sustain perfusion.

Heart failure is characterized by

TypeDescription
Forward failureDiminished cardiac output
Backward failureDamming back of blood in the venous system (principally in the lung parenchyma)
Both (most instances)Biventricular forward and backward failure: failure on one side is transmitted to the other side
  • Over time → fibrosis, dilatation, and change in LV shape from elliptical to spherical
  • Reduced CO → underperfusion and arterial underfilling → ↓ oxygen perfusion in cells and tissues

D. Compensatory Mechanisms p. 7-8

Three Compensatory Mechanisms to Maintain CO, Arterial Pressure, and Perfusion Must Know

1. Frank-Starling mechanism

2. Myocardial adaptations

3. Activation of neurohumoral systems

  • Release of NE by ANS
  • Activation of RAAS
  • Release of ANP: adjusts filling volumes and pressure through diuresis and natriuresis
Exam trapCompensation includes an increase in heart rate, not a decrease.
Elaboration of corticosteroids by adrenal gland is NOT one of the compensatory mechanisms. Review / formative keys

1. Frank-Starling Mechanism

  • The greater the volume of blood entering the heart during diastole (end diastolic volume), the greater the volume ejected during systole (stroke volume)
Dilatation
→
↑ Preload
→
↑ Contractility
→
↑ CO
  • Increased preload dilates the heart → ↑ actin-myosin cross bridge formation → enhanced contractility and stroke volume
  • Physiological importance: maintaining left and right ventricular output equality, plays a role in compensation of systolic heart failure

In heart failure

↓ Preload and stroke volume → incomplete LV emptying
↓
Blood accumulating in LV during diastole is greater than normal
↓
Amplified residual volume ↑ stretch of myocardial fibers → greater stroke volume next contraction
↓
Better emptying of the large ventricle → preserves and augments CO

2. Myocardial Adaptations

  • Myocardial hypertrophy with or without cardiac chamber dilatation
    • LV hypertrophy → increased contractility
    • LV remodeling → increased stroke volume (new sarcomeres, change in cell length and width)
  • Heart failure is usually preceded by cardiac muscle hypertrophy, achieved by ventricular remodeling
  • Ventricular remodeling: collective molecular, cellular, and structural changes in the ventricular wall
  • Sustained pressure or volume overload → myocytes increase in size = cellular hypertrophy
  • Hypertrophy requires ↑ protein synthesis, ↑ mitochondria → enlarged myocyte with multiple enlarged nuclei
Key progressionInitially, these adaptive mechanisms maintain adequate CO.
Progressively, the muscle becomes tired and fatigued, and intractable heart failure sets in.
Progressive deterioration of contractile function = systolic dysfunction → ↓ ejection fraction.

3. Activation of Neurohumoral Systems

Sympathetic nervous system

  • Release of NE / E → ↑ HR → ↑ contraction
  • Activation of high and low pressure baroreceptors: early compensation providing inotropic support
  • Chronic sympathetic activation has deleterious effects → further deterioration of cardiac function
    • Activates RAAS → ↑ venous and arterial flow → ↑ preload and afterload
    • ↑ plasma noradrenaline, progressive retention of salt and water → edema
    • Associated with myocyte apoptosis, hypertrophy, and focal myocardial necrosis

RAAS

  • ↑ renin, plasma angiotensin II, and aldosterone
  • Angiotensin II: potent vasoconstrictor of renal afferent arterioles and systemic circulation, stimulates noradrenaline release
    • → Retention of sodium and water and increased excretion of potassium
    • May contribute to endothelial dysfunction in chronic HF

Natriuretic peptides

  • ANP: released from the atria in response to stretch → natriuresis and vasodilatation
  • BNP: released predominantly from the ventricle, actions similar to ANP
  • ANP and BNP ↑ with volume expansion and pressure overload → act as physiological antagonists to angiotensin II
Key pointMost neurohumoral responses are compensatory in the early stages of HF.
But may further exacerbate the increased afterload and stress on the already failing heart.

E. Pathophysiology of CHF p. 8-9

Cardiac Hypertrophy: Two Patterns Must Know

Cardiac hypertrophy: initial compensatory response of the myocardium to increase the force of contraction and mechanical work.

Pressure overloadVolume overload
CausesHPN and valvular stenosisValvular regurgitations: AR / MR
PatternConcentric hypertrophyHypertrophy and dilatation
Wall / cavity↑ ventricular wall thickness
Reduced cavity diameter		↑ ventricular diameter
Wall thickness may be increased, normal or less than normal
SarcomeresAssembled in parallel to the long axis → expands cross-sectional area of myocytesAssembled in series within existing sarcomeres → ventricular dilatation
Exam trapPressure overload does NOT increase ventricular diameter. It reduces cavity diameter.
In dilated hearts, heart weight rather than wall thickness is the best measure of hypertrophy.
Why the hypertrophied heart failsMyocyte hypertrophy is not accompanied by a proportional increase in capillary numbers → O₂ and nutrient supply compromised.
Hypertrophy ↑ metabolic demand and O₂ consumption.
Hence, the hypertrophied heart is vulnerable to ischemia-related decompensation → cardiac failure.

Gross and Microscopic Changes

  • Prominent clinical manifestation: cardiomegaly (biventricular enlargement, dilatation, hypertrophy)
  • Dilatation and hypertrophy are more evident in the left ventricle

Basis for Myocardial Contractile Failure

Features expressed in the ventricular remodeling pathway in HF:

  • Death of myocytes and loss of vital elements of pump
  • Overworked and fatigued cardiac muscles
  • With prolonged hemodynamic overload, gene expression is altered
  • Re-expression of protein synthesis equal to that in fetal cardiac development

Anatomic, Biochemical, and Ultrastructural Changes

Pathologic hypertrophy

  • Increased protein synthesis
  • Altered gene expression → induction of fetal gene program
  • Synthesis of abnormal contractile protein → protein isoforms that reduce excitation-coupling
  • Increased fibrosis with reduced vasculature

Decreased calcium levels and mitochondrial function

Microcirculatory spasm

Increased apoptosis
→
Loss of myocytes
→
Myocardial dysfunction

Left-Sided Heart Failure p. 10-13

Definition and Causes Must Know

  • Failure occurs when there is intrinsic dysfunction of the left side of the heart → insufficient delivery of blood to vital body organs
📣 Causes of left-sided HFIschemic heart disease (IHD), Hypertension, Acute Myocardial Infarction, Aortic/Mitral Valve diseases, Primary diseases of the left ventricle.
All diseases primarily affect the left ventricle.
Exam trapPulmonary embolism is NOT a cause of left-sided HF. It is a cause of isolated right-sided HF.
  • Effects are a consequence of passive congestion with blood backing up in the pulmonary circulation, stasis in left chambers, and inadequate perfusion of downstream tissues

Types of Left-Sided HF: Systolic vs Diastolic Must Know

Classified on the basis of the level of abnormalities in the ejection fraction.

Systolic dysfunction / failureDiastolic dysfunction / failure
CausesIHD, Hypertensive Heart Disease, CardiomyopathyMassive LV hypertrophy with marked reduction of ventricular cavity
Infiltrative / restrictive lesions: amyloidosis, myocardial elastosis, constrictive pericarditis
Valvular: mitral stenosis
Myocardial fibrosis
PathophysiologyImpaired myocardial contractile function = ↓ ejection fraction and ↓ cardiac outputImpaired diastolic filling, inability of chamber to expand sufficiently in diastole
LV is abnormally stiff and cannot relax
EF and CODecreased
Normal EF = 45-65%		Normal / slightly reduced
ChamberHeart muscles thinned, chambers dilatedSmaller ventricular chamber, ventricular hypertrophy, poor compliance
ClinicalMost common type of HF
LV failure and cardiomegaly

Cardiac function relatively preserved at rest
Cannot maximize output with increased demand
LV cannot expand normally
→
↑ filling pressure transferred back to pulmonary circulation
→
Pulmonary edema

Pathophysiology of Left-Sided HF

Pressure overload

  • Systemic HPN → ↑ workload → LVH (initially compensatory) → long term inhibits relaxation → concentric hypertrophy, reduced LV chamber → impaired filling, ↓ LV output
  • Coronary arterial diseases → direct ischemic damage → remodeling and scar formation → ↓ contractility and CO
  • Aortic stenosis → LVH due to increased workload against a gradient along the obstructed aortic valve
  • Cardiomyopathies → variable mechanisms causing cardiac stiffness and dysfunction

Volume overload

  • Increased LV workload from aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, and congenital heart diseases that allow shunting of blood

Morphology of Left-Sided HF Must Know

OrganFindings
HeartDepends on underlying primary cardiac disease: coagulative necrosis in acute MI, valvular defects of aortic and mitral valves, intrinsic myocardial pathology
KidneysRelease of RAAS → edema and vascular congestion
BrainHypoxic encephalopathy, particularly in uncompensated HF
Red neurons (dead neuronal cells), cerebral edema, congestion
Lungs 📣The lungs bear the brunt of anatomic changes where accumulation of fluids primarily occur
Pulmonary congestion and edema are characteristic
Pleural transudative serous effusions
Heavy wet lungs that exude water on cut section
📣 Acute vs Chronic left ventricular HFIn Acute Left Ventricular HF → Acute Pulmonary Edema.
In Chronic Left Ventricular HF → Chronic Passive Congestion.
Exam trapAcute liver congestion is NOT a feature of acute, pure left-sided HF, where the lungs are primarily affected.

Kerley B Lines

  • Perivascular and interstitial edema of the interlobular septae → characteristic Kerley B and C lines on x-ray
  • Kerley B lines
    • Thin horizontal lines 1-2 cm in length in the periphery of the lungs
    • Represent engorgement and edema of the lymphatic vessels or edema of the interlobular septa
    • Usually occur when pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is elevated, reaching 20-25 mmHg

Acute Pulmonary Edema vs Chronic Passive Congestion

Heart failure cellsHistiocytes that contain ingested yellow-brown hemosiderin pigment.
RBC escapes into the air sac → breaks down → iron liberated → phagocytosed by macrophages.
Pathognomonic of chronic passive congestion and CHF associated with increased alveolar capillary pressures.
Can also be seen in other diseases (pulmonary infarction or hemorrhage).

Mechanism of pulmonary edema and congestion

Underfilling and poor myocardial contractility → ↓ CO
↓
Damming of blood in the LV → ↑ ventricular hydrostatic pressure
↓
↑ pressure reflected in the pulmonary capillaries
↓
Transudative effusion and alveolar edema

Clinical Features of Left-Sided HF Must Know

FeatureKey points
DyspneaSubjective shortness of breath, usually the first symptom of HF
Characteristically effort related = exertional dyspnea
OrthopneaPosition-dependent SOB when lying flat
Basis: ↑ venous return from legs and GI veins to the lungs on lying flat
PNDSudden urgent SOB during sleep from progressive pulmonary venous congestion
Characteristic sign of left ventricular failure
Rales, cough, "rusty" sputum↑ pulmonary venous pressure → recurrent alveolar hemorrhages
Rusty brown sputum = hemosiderin-laden macrophages
Crackles and rales in the dependent portions of the lungs
↑ HR, cardiomegaly, ↑ JVPDistension of superficial jugular vein in semi-erect position: one of the earliest signs of CHF
LV dilatation on x-ray / echo
Tachycardia: adaptive sympathetic response
Central venous congestion, edemaRenal fluid retention → ↑ venous return and preload
Liver may be enlarged (CPC), abnormal LFTs
Pre-renal azotemiaKidney hypoperfused → elevated serum BUN and creatinine
Cyanosis, hypoxic encephalopathyFar advanced CHF → cerebral hypoperfusion → irritability, restlessness → stupor and coma
DiagnosisNo routine laboratory test is helpful in the diagnosis of heart failure.
Echocardiography remains the gold standard.
BNP is increased in early heart failure, likely to become a routine test.

Right-Sided Heart Failure p. 13-14

Definition and Causes Must Know

  • Failure of the right side (ventricle): RV hypertrophy/dilatation and RA dilatation
  • Most commonly caused by left-sided heart failure (biventricular heart failure)
    • ↑ pulmonary pressure from left-sided HF burdens the right side → causes of right-sided HF include all etiology of left-sided HF

Causes of pure isolated right-sided HF

  • Pulmonary embolism (acute/chronic) 📣
    • Thromboembolism ↑ pulmonary artery pressure → reflected back to the RV
    • Acute pulmonary embolism: Dilates
    • Chronic pulmonary embolism: adaptive response → ventricle becomes thickened (hypertrophic)
  • Intrinsic lung disease (COPD, cystic fibrosis)
  • Pulmonary HPN (primary/secondary)
  • Others: kyphoscoliosis, pneumoconiosis, schistosomiasis
Fibrosis and/or hypoxic vascular response
→
↑ pulmonary vascular resistance = pulmonary hypertension
→
Dilatation of the right side, particularly the ventricle
Major clinical effect of primary right-sided HFMinimal pulmonary congestion.
More pronounced engorgement of systemic and portal venous system.

Morphology of Right-Sided HF Must Know

OrganFindings
HeartRV dilation / hypertrophy, varies with cause
Rarely structural defects (tricuspid / pulmonary valve)
Since most cases are from intrinsic lung disease → only hypertrophy and dilation of RA and RV
LungsPure right-sided HF: not wet, no pulmonary edema
LiverCongestive hepatomegaly due to CPC → "nutmeg liver"
Centrilobular necrosis when congestion is severe
Cardiac cirrhosis in long-standing right-sided HF
SpleenCongestive splenomegaly
KidneyRenal congestion more severe in right-sided HF → greater fluid retention and peripheral edema
BrainVenous congestion and hypoxia → deficit in mental function
OthersSystemic congestion, effusions (pleural, peritoneal, pericardial)
Subcutaneous edema: ankle, presacral, pretibial
📣 Acute vs Chronic right-sided HFAcute right-sided HF → RV dilation due to sudden pressure overload. Not hypertrophic since there was no time for the heart to adapt.
Chronic right-sided HF → adaptive mechanism includes becoming hypertrophic. Dilation follows.

Gross and Microscopic Figures

Clinical Features of Right-Sided HF

  • Splanchnic congestion: hepato-splenomegaly
    • PE: pitting peripheral edema, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly
  • Elevated JVP, accentuated by the hepatojugular reflex → jugular venous distention
  • Transudative effusions: widespread dependent edema, anasarca in severe cases
Key differentiatorIn pure right-sided HF, lungs may not exhibit crackles because there is no pulmonary edema.

Combined Left and Right-Sided HF p. 14-15

  • RV and LV share a common interventricular septum and function on a closed circuit
    • Failure of one ventricle is inevitably followed by failure in the other → both fall in tandem
  • Failure on the left may secondarily affect the other side through time → biventricular HF
📣 Terminal eventIn chronic cardiac decompensation with biventricular CHF: both RV and LV become dilated and enlarged.

High Output vs Low Output Heart Failure p. 15

High Output Heart Failure 📣 Must Know

  • HF secondary to pumping excessive volume of blood (higher CO) due to higher peripheral demand
  • Patients may have normal cardiac function and decreased systemic vascular resistance
    • The problem lies with the increase in the body's demand for perfusion
  • Less common type of heart failure
Cause categoryExamples
IatrogenicOverload situations like high blood or serum infusion
Hypermetabolic statesHyperthyroidism and high fever
Nutritional statesVitamin B deficiency (e.g., Cardiac Beriberi)
Shunting anomaliesArteriovenous malformations
Lecturer-cited 📣Hyperthyrotoxicosis, anemia

Low Output Heart Failure

  • Clinical syndrome of decreased cardiac output accompanied by end-organ hypoperfusion
  • Uncommon in the general population, but prevalent in post-operation HF patients
  • Causes: AMI, HPN, congenital HD, valvular HD, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, drug defects, electrical imbalance
Exam trapHypothyroidism → ↓ thyroid hormone → ↓ metabolic demand and cardiac contractility → low output HF.
Do not confuse with hyperthyroidism / anemia / AV shunts → high output HF. Formative quiz key

Summary

Heart failure occurs when the heart is unable to provide the adequate adaptive mechanisms to satisfy the perfusion and metabolic requirements of peripheral tissues. This leads to inadequate cardiac output accompanied by a constellation of morphological tissue changes and clinical manifestations.

❗ Red-Flag Points

  • Ischemic Heart Disease: 1 of the most important disease in modern urban population
    • Obstruction of coronary flow by occluding thrombus or atheroma
  • Lambl's excrescences: hallmark = poorly vascularized, dense, fibrous CT
  • Case scenario: the absence of fever rules out an infectious/inflammatory cause

Core Definitions

  • Heart failure: complex clinical syndrome from any structural or functional cardiac disorder that impairs the ventricle to refill or eject blood
    • A syndrome, not a disease · final common pathway · clinical diagnosis
  • Hypertrophy = ↑ weight or wall thickness · Dilation = enlarged chamber · Cardiomegaly = hypertrophy and/or dilation · Atrophy = ↓ size and function
  • Ventricular remodeling: collective molecular, cellular, structural changes in the ventricular wall

Mechanisms

6 mechanisms of cardiac dysfunction

Pump failure · Obstruction · Regurgitation · Shunted flow · Conduction disorders · Rupture (→ tamponade)

3 compensatory mechanisms

Frank-Starling
dilatation → ↑ preload → ↑ contractility → ↑ CO
+
Myocardial adaptations
LVH → ↑ contractility
remodeling → ↑ SV
+
Neurohumoral
NE (↑ HR) · RAAS (Na/water retention) · ANP/BNP (antagonize Ang II)
  • Persistently elevated in CHF: NE, renin, ADH
  • Early = compensatory → late = ↑ afterload and stress on failing heart

Pathologic hypertrophy → failure

↑ protein synthesis, fetal gene program, abnormal isoforms, fibrosis
→
↓ Ca and mitochondrial function, microcirculatory spasm
→
↑ apoptosis → loss of myocytes → dysfunction
  • Hypertrophy without proportional ↑ capillaries → vulnerable to ischemia-related decompensation

Diagnostic Anchors and Warnings

  • Echocardiography = gold standard for HF diagnosis · BNP ↑ in early HF
  • Troponin and tropomyosin = sensitive and specific markers of cardiac injury (AMI)
  • Earliest sign of CHF: jugular vein distension in semi-erect position · first symptom: dyspnea
  • Aging change with greatest impact: LV wall contractility · greatest valve change: aortic
  • Fatty streak is NOT an aging finding · corticosteroid elaboration is NOT a CHF compensation · PE is NOT a cause of left-sided HF
  • Terminal event in biventricular CHF: both RV and LV dilated and enlarged
